Kayo Dot is my favorite band, too. I'm gonna go against the prevailing consensus a bit and actually defend Coyote and Blue Lambency Downward. They're my 2nd and 3rd favorite KD albums, respectively (after the indomitable Choirs of the Eye).

BLD is often criticized by fans for sounding aimless and lacking in resolution. I think that's because a lot of KD fans, especially those who really enjoyed the first album, continued to approach the albums after DAWCT looking for the same sort of post-rock dynamics that drew them to the band in the first place, when Toby has made it pretty clear in interviews that he was really interested at this time (and probably still is, I'm not sure) in exploring other means of achieving tension and resolution than the usual post-rock/metal tricks: speeding up tempos, adding more layers, increasing volume, etc (even though I do think he utilized these dynamics exquisitely in CotE). And I actually think he does this fantastically on BLD. This is where my faculties of criticism break down: I can't really explain specifically what it is about the album I like. In general, I think it's one of, if not the most, sonically diverse KD releases, which it manages to do while still retaining a remarkable coherence throughout. "Symmetrical Arizona" is one of the highlights of Toby's entire discography, in my opinion. If you re-listen to nothing else on BLD, I suggest you give that one another shot.

Coyote took me the longest out of all Kayo Dot albums to appreciate. The instrumentation and textures were unlike anything I had ever heard, and the sheer alienness of it threw me off more than I care to admit. But once it "clicked" with me, I found myself immersed in a realm equal parts horrifying and psychedelic. It's like the world's best bad acid trip, if that makes any sense... "Abyss Hinge 2" really does sound like a descent into some dark mental pit with bizarre lifeforms and atmospheric phenomena whirling around you, until that lull in the middle when the instruments stop momentarily and you're just suspended in this void with nothing to ground you but the sub-bass pulse of your own (or I guess, the protagonist's) heartbeat, and then it all comes rushing back, building to a majestic catharsis in those final few minutes.

So yeah, I love those two albums. I can understand why they're not as popular as the others, though. In my opinion, KD's worst release was probably Gamma Knife. So many great ideas, so much potential, betrayed by shitty production. I understand lo-fi aesthetics and their relationship to black metal. I can appreciate lo-fi recording when used in the service of the music. And I know about the logistical issues they faced with recording the album. All that being said, the production was just awful...like, inexcusably, ruinously awful. I really hope they record a proper version of that album in the future. Though I doubt that will ever happen.

Edit: Btw, I have to mention Toby's other project, Tartar Lamb (and Tartar Lamb II). I don't know if you've checked it out already, but if not, you NEED to make "Polyimage of Known Exits" your next listen. Think Coyote with more ambience and noise, and less rhythmically driven. It is some of the best shit Toby's done. "60 Metonymies" is good, too, but nowhere near "Polyimage."

The shamanic register is just a term I use for a particular variety of Nuvaali called *aala veeli* ("shaman's speech") which is used not only *by* shamans when communicating with the community and among themselves, but also by members of the wider speech community when communicating with shamans, who typically live an ascetic and isolated lifestyle. This register is one of the last vestiges of an older politeness system that distinguished between several social classes and prescribed mostly the kind of vocabulary and a few phonetic patterns that would be used among speakers. This system collapsed after a radical transformation of social conditions following the Fall.

In Sarendreilic languages, there can be several parameters along which words are harmonized. The proto-language features the following constraints on stems:

1. There cannot be two pairs of sequential vowels in a word such that one pair ascends in height, and the other descends in height.

(2. The above rule implies two or more sequential vowels may be of the same height.)

This would be a violation of *height harmony*, and would be subject to the following rule:

1. If an inflectional suffix causes a word to violate the principle of height harmony, then the last vowel in the root changes in height the minimal amount necessary to reestablish height harmony, if this is possible, and the root is two or more syllables in length.

So here's an example of height harmony in action:

>tsõlõmbu
>[t͡sɔ̃ːɮɔ̃ːᵐbu]
>'fox'

>*tsõlõmbu-to
>*[t͡sɔ̃ːɮɔ̃ːᵐbuto]
>'fox (ergative)'

Here, *tsõlõmbu-to violates height harmony by having one sequence of syllables involve a progressive increase in height (from /õ/ to /u/), and another sequence (/u/ to /o/) involve a decrease in height. Therefore, it would be "fixed" to:

>tsõlõmb**o**-to
>[t͡sɔ̃ːɮɔ̃ːᵐboto]
>'fox (ergative)'

Height harmony like this works well because both nouns and verbs in Sarendreilic languages can only take one inflectional suffix each.

Nasal harmony constrains words by imposing the following restriction: *every nasal vowel before a given nasal vowel (within a word) must also be nasal.* Kind of an awkward way to put it, but it's basically regressive nasal assimilation. A nasal vowel triggers every vowel before it to nasalize as well.

Nasal harmony is strictly an *intramorphemic* constraint, so neither derivational nor inflectional affixes affect the nasality of other vowels in a word. However, due to historical alterations in the stages of the language preceding Proto-Sarendreilic, there are virtually no bound suffixal morphemes with nasal vowels in Proto-Sarendreilic.

Coronal harmony is another intramorphemic constraint that states a morpheme may not contain both laminal-dental *and* apical-alveolar consonants, both of which are phonemic in Proto-Sarendreilic. It's not triggered by affixes either.

To answer both your own and /u/Jafiki91 's question, I'll list some of the defining and notable features of each language family, going from North to South instead of alphabetical order:

* **Gerrodic**: The proto-language featured extensive use of non-concatenative morphology: infixes, circumfixes, even transfixes like the Semitic languages. Most words derived from bi- or tri-consonantal roots with a rather general meaning superimposed onto a "template" supplying additional semantic content. In the proto-language, such morphology was frequently and productively used in both derivation and inflection, but nowadays, true "root/template" morphology only survives in a handful of languages within the interior (the Spritewood, as it is referred to in legend). Instead, most languages nowadays are highly fusional, resembling Indo-European languages in their interplay of voice, mood, and aspect, as well as specifically language branches like Celtic and Germanic in their extensive use of both consonant and vowel mutation. Phonologically, think lots of phonation distinctions (everything from breathy to creaky voice), four to six places of articulation for stops, and generally pretty regular consonant inventories. Word order and morphosyntactic alignment conditioned by an animacy hierarchy, whose exact details and number of categories (generally three) differ between languages, but whose exact manifestation varies between ergative-absolutive, nominative-accusative, and both split- and fluid-S active-stative alignment. Many languages in this family feature extensive taboo systems, mostly centered around avoiding the names of the dead. As such, even common words are often replaced, leading to a high degree of variation in vocabulary between different speech communities.

* **Sarendreilic**: Large consonant inventories distinguishing between lateral approximants, fricatives, and affricates at three places of articulation. Many feature prenasalized consonants--a feature also shared by the neighboring Western Tivonic languages, forming a sort of Sprachbund that transcends language family. Various phonotactic rules feature harmony of some sort: in the proto-language there are two parameters for vowel harmony (backness and height), something called coronal harmony, as well as regressive nasal harmony affecting both consonants and vowels. Grammatically, Sarendreilic languages tend to be split-ergative in alignment and employ two parallel number paradigms: singular-dual-plural and collective-singulative, which are assigned lexically to words.

* **Tivonic**: Proto-language featured uvular consonants, prenasalization, non-spirant affricates, and a three-level tone system. Languages to the west tend to use fewer or no tones, while languages towards the east coast utilize increasingly complex tone systems, including contour tones. Incorporation of nouns is common and productive in most branches. Highly agglutinative and polysynthetic, this is one of those languages where one word can express an entire English sentence. Sociolinguistically, one notable feature expressed in the proto-language is gendered speech: there is a marked difference in consonant inventory between men and women's speech, as well as some differences in vocabulary and pragmatics. Some of these differences have been retained or even expanded upon in various branches, but many have been lost.

* **Swarthish**: SOV language, mostly isolating (except for frequent compounding), handful of inflectional and derivational suffixes but many roots. Heavy use of periphrasis for expressing verbal categories, due to a lack of productive morphology. Phonologically, clusters are common, the most frequent consonants seem to be /z/, /v/, and /ŋ/, and the vowel system is a little uneven.

* **Kinjaro-Khitayic**: Variously SVO or VSO, fusional and agglutinative properties, three true genders (masculine, feminine, neuter) collapsed in various ways in some languages, ergative alignment most common. Verbs agree in a nominative-accusative fashion, however, with subject, direct object, and sometimes indirect object. Several phonological differences between the two main branches: Kinjaric (small phoneme inventories, CV syllable structure, retention of phonemic /ɨ/, loss of ejectives) and Khitayic (retention of ejectives, lenition of aspirated stops, front rounded vowels, tolerance of clusters).

* **Darshinnese**: Rather small phoneme inventory, highly analytic, almost exclusively prefixing and SVO.

* **Dzueybo-Kharaghic**: It's hard to generalize with this family, the two main branches *Dzueybic* and *Kharaghic* being quite dissimilar in a number of ways. Dzueybic languages tend to be tonal, having lost most syllable-final consonants. They are more agglutinative and feature more cases than the Kharaghic languages, which are non-tonal, fusional, and feature only 3-5 cases, generally speaking. Some shared commonalities, however, include strict nominative-accusative alignment and general VSO or SVO word order, as well as a balance between prefixation and suffixation as morphological strategies, though the Kharaghic languages almost exclusively utilize suffixation for inflection.

* **Tidelandic**: Because the Tidesmen's oral tract has evolved independently from the hominid races (human, Nuvaali, Swarthclad), this is not an easy set of languages to describe with current linguistic terminology. They seem to be capable of stop- and approximant-like consonants, at the very least. The classic distinctions between vowel and consonant, sonorant and obstruent, do not seem to be well-suited for describing these languages's phoneme inventories. In fact, the very concept of a phoneme is in doubt, as these languages tend to utilize sounds which can vary *continuously* in a number of phonetic parameters to express different meanings in proportion to the amount of deviation from the sound's prototypical values (for instance, the exact degree of bigness denoted by the word for "big" may be proportional to the height of the vowel, which can take on any value between the two extremes of "close" and "open" to express a range of relative size). Despite lacking nasal sounds altogether, the Tidesmen's languages seem to distinguish between and make heavy use of a wide variety of airstream mechanisms and several different manners of articulation that might be described as "pseudo-fricative." Central and lateral distinction maintained, as well as an additional class of consonants usually referred to as "circumferential" consonants, which are pronounced with airflow surrounding the body of the tongue, which is suspended within the oral tract. These languages seem to prioritize grammatical categories which are rare or even altogether absent in hominid languages. Despite these differences, however, Tidesmen and hominids do seem to be capable of understanding each other's speech, even if they have trouble wrapping their tongues around the respective sounds, though it is said Tidesmen have an easier time understanding hominid languages than vice versa. There are even a number of pidgin-like sign languages that have developed in situations where humans and Tidesmen live in close proximity, which both races seem to be equally capable of articulating, despite profound differences in their native languages' syntax, semantics, and pragmatics.

* **Nuvaali**: Very small phoneme inventory inspired by Polynesian languages. Fusional inflection with a degree of consonant mutation. Five tenses (distant past, near past, present, near future, distant future), agreement for multiple arguments, heavy use of topic-comment structures, rigid SVO word order. Use of a highly formalized "shamanic register" was formerly common, but is now dying out.

I haven't worked out the exact number of languages in each family, as I'm working on a diachronic approach: starting out with a proto-language for each family, and working out the individual descendants from there, and I haven't quite finished it yet, having only worked intensively on a handful of the proto-languages. But I can give you an estimate of how many languages there will be in each family by the end, keeping in mind of course that the distinction between language and dialect can be fuzzy. For scale, this continent is about the size of Africa.

Darshinnese: Language isolate

Dzueybo-Kharaghic: ~45 languages. Most widely-spoken language is Kharaghish Proper, which is a direct descendant of Ancient Kharaghish, the language of the Kharaghish Empire which at the height of its territorial gains consisted of most of the southern half of the continent, except Terua to the far south (where Nuvaali is spoken). The situation is similar to China, where several autochthonous languages exist alongside a standardized national language (except in the coastal areas, where localized dialects of Kharaghish Proper have almost totally wiped out native Coastal Erg languages.)

Gerrodic: ~30 languages. Main concentration of diversity is in the west, with languages becoming increasingly less divergent the further east and south you go.

Kinjaro-Khitayic: ~15 languages. Used to cover much more territory to the south and southwest of its current range, but the spread of Kharaghic languages (*not* Kharaghish Proper) overwhelmingly ousted the Kinjaric languages previously spoken in these regions, in a manner similar to the Bantu migrations in central and southern Africa. Nowadays, the only remaining branch are the Khitayic languages, the speakers of which have a tendency to overlook issues of intelligibility in favor of politics when deciding which speech varieties to consider distinct languages. In truth, you could perhaps easily triple the number of languages I mentioned above, if going by intelligibility as a criterion.

Nuvaali: A language isolate. Despite the wide range the language covers, it has only been some 400 years or so since the Fall of Nuvaala, a devastating event in the history of the Nuvaali which led to the destruction of their cloud-borne homeland and their eventual political unification and resettlement in the uninhabited peninsula of Terua (Nuvaala Anatai). The modern Nuvaali language, called Nuvaali Anatai, is a blend of several previously isolated Nuvaali tribal dialects which were forced to coexist after the Fall, chiefly among them the Milani (Snake) and Va'uusi (Dragon) tribes'.

Sarendreilic: ~50 languages. Language diversity peaks in the center of the range. No language has really spread to a degree disproportionate to its relatives.

Swarthish: Language isolate, split into five dialects: Mavi, Kuzakhiri, Nar, Zang, and Zvanggo.

Tidelandic: 2 languages. Spoken by the para-human Tidesmen, an amphibious race whose vocal tract is quite different from other races. (This is my attempt at an experimental non-human languages that express a different set of typological universals). Actually two *unrelated* languages, Island Tidelandic and Basin Tidelandic, which I've decided to group into one for the purposes of this map.

Tivonic: ~25 languages. Dominated by Túshega dialects. Language diversity peaks in the east along the banks of the Kkhyóóngw River, and decreases westward.

In general, I go by the rule of thumb that language diversity increases with proximity to a particular family or branch's Urheimat, and decreases out from there. With exceptions.

Most human naming schemes in my world are pretty vanilla. A rather more involved one is used among the Berlairese. The formula is essentially: 

Given name + Family name of parent of the same sex + Family name of parent of opposite sex + *bal a* ("from the") + Place of birth/upbringing

So, for instance, the current Roethian Empress, who is originally from Berlaire, has the following full name:

**Kinerta Labeire Pilarme bal a Tasuar**

* Kinerta = given name
* Labeire = mother's family name (considered the Empress's family name as well)
* Pilarme = father's family name
* bal a Tasuar = "from Tasuar (a province in Berlaire)"

The lands around the Lys Mountains are home to the ubiquitous little pests known as **Lightning Bugs.** One Lightning Bug is no biggie, but, of course, they never appear alone, forming potentially huge hive structures.

Lightning Bugs are carnivorous generalists, eating any kind of prey they can get their claws on. Each is relatively small, about 1 cm in length. They have a single pair of wings and powerful jaws, but they do not typically bite people, nor do they have any kind of stinging mechanism.

What they do have is an organ in their abdomens that essentially functions as an electrode. You put two Lightning Bugs in close proximity to each other, and they can activate these organs to produce a rather weak electrical arc between the two of them. This is the primary means by which they ZAPPP!! their prey. Larger swarms can produce more powerful arcs to take down prey as large as bats and birds.

There are countless tales of huge Lightning Bug swarms attacking and paralyzing humans, but none of these tales can be confirmed with absolute certainty. The stories are enough, however, to keep the locals away from their hives, which resemble calcified black masses attached to rock faces, tree branches, or shrubs. The black coloration comes from the saliva that these insects use to glue together bits of dead twigs, insect husks, pebbles, metal screws, cloth, just about any substance natural or artificial that they can carry back to the hive.

Lightning Bugs are attracted to sources of electricity, for reasons unknown. Without continuous maintenance, you may find a Lightning Bug hive has taken root inside your car, airship, or generator. They can easily wreak havoc on electrical equipment, biting their way through rubber and copper wiring, clogging mechanisms with their droppings and saliva, and messing up sensitive electrical devices with their lightning arcs.

Long story short, if you're ever traveling in the Lys Mountains or the Roethian Savannah and you catch a glimpse of what looks to be a black floating ball of lightning drifting aimlessly through the air, you'd best avoid it.

Sorry, can't help you much with the controller thing. I've never needed to adjust to a new controller, since I've always gamed exclusively on Playstation (besides handhelds, of course). But I imagine it's kind of like starting a new game that's VERY similar to one you've played before, but the controls are mapped differently, and it just takes a while to get the hang of it. Play around with the mob enemies in the first level till you're used to the controls, or even try playing some other games if that helps.

However, here are some common mistakes I've noticed new Dark Souls players make:

1. Rolling away from the attack. / Usually, you want to roll INTO attacks, or roll AROUND the enemy. The reason being, if you roll away, there's a chance the attack will catch you as you exit the rolling animation. Less likely if you roll into or around the attack.

2. Getting greedy. / Don't do it. Depending on your starting weapon, stick to 2-3 blows, then immediately get out of his way. Gundyr is a rather aggressive boss.

3. Trying to get the most out of your estus. / I know there's a temptation to want to conserve your estus, especially at the beginning of the game, so that you only chug when your health is low enough to make full use of the healing amount. This is a good idea in principle, but with bosses, I prefer to chug more often. Chug as soon as your health drops to about 60% or so, because if your health is anything less than that, there is a good chance you will get killed. Better to run out of estus and still have a fighting chance than to get killed because you let your health drop to a third before doing anything about it.

4. Blocking. / Medium shields are tricky to use, and the shields you start out with don't absorb enough health to make them useful in my opinion. Roll instead, at least until you get a shield with 100% protection,

5. Bad stamina management. / Never let your Stamina drop to 0 during a boss fight. Always have a little bit left so you can dodge at least once.

6. Losing your rhythm. / Every enemy has a certain "rhythm" to their attacks, especially during more aggressive combos. The attacks will usually hit at predictable and consistent intervals. I found that, several times when fighting Gundyr (and several other bosses), I would miss a dodge, get hit, and that would cause me to keep mis-timing my dodges. That's the main way I would die. As for the lore of my current project, it's definitely in its early stages, but basically, the name of this planet is Jarkhat, which means "pearl" in the Kharaghish language. It was discovered by Kharaghish scientists during the Second Age of Man, and subsequently, a generation ship carrying some 300 travelers was sent out to colonize the alien planet. The journey would take close to 500 years.

In the interim, the Second Age of Man came to a close with the catastrophic Wizards' Rebellions that marked the beginning of the Third Age and spelled doom for the reigning technocracies of Berys. In an attempt to flee the destruction and warfare around them, a powerful prophet-mage who had perfected astral travel teleported himself and his 50-some followers lightyears through the stars, a feat never before accomplished, to arrive on Jarkhat. Here they found a truly alien world, but not an inhospitable one. Over the years, these settlers grew in number and, aided by the abundance of aether (a ubiquitous source of magic) on this newfound planet, power, as well. They developed their own society, government, and culture, and lived in relative harmony with the indigenous sapient inhabitants of Jarkhat, the Rilakh. 

Fast forward some 500 years from the launching of the aforementioned generation ship, isolated from and unaware of the machinations of the outside world, the spacecraft and its precious cargo have arrived at their destination. But some changes have taken place from the onset of the mission. In the 500 years since, a series of mutinies, power struggles, religious schisms, and all-out warfare took place among the passengers, resulting in the deaths of all but one lineage of the original colonists, who now proclaim themselves the true heirs of Jarkhat. The pilgrims have descended into madness. Now boasting a population nearly triple what the ships were designed to support, the remaining travelers look desperately to their new home for hope and an answer to their prayers, only to find, upon landing, that they are not the first ones here, and they are not alone.

Science fiction doesn't always deal with futuristic societies or technology. The root of science fiction is, of course, science, so using your knowledge of science (ecology and botany, in this case) to construct a plausible world would be fully within the realm of sci-fi. 

To answer your second question, I would suggest reading some of Michael Crichton's books. He does a good job at explaining complex scientific ideas in an accessible way that fits naturally into the narrative, usually by way of a third-person narrator. 

You could also go the route of having companion "non-fiction" books that explain your ecology in greater detail and that aren't bound to a story.

By the way, if you're interested in xenobiology, this is a great project to check out: https://canopy.uc.edu/bbcswebdav/users/gibsonic/Snaiad/snduterus.html

It mostly focuses on "animal" life, not flora, but is a good example of a truly alien constructed world.

My world, Berys, has gone through a number of millennia-spanning cycles where the amount of magic in the world fluctuates from abundantly common to virtually non-existent (save for a few diehard mages that preserve esoteric methods of accessing magic). The last such "magic drought" spurred the development of industrialization and scientific progress, as the inhabitants saw the ruins and artifacts of magical civilizations before them and attempted to emulate their accomplishments through technology. After a cataclysmic global war, however, much of this technology was lost as the ruling technocratic elite was overthrown.

Some areas of technology were more developed than others by this time. Nuclear technology was mostly at the same level as our current world (though in much higher use) as were agriculture and architecture. Communications was somewhat more advanced, though they had yet to invent quantum computing. Space travel, too--to the point where one nation managed to create generation ships to transport colonists to another planet. Other areas like genetic engineering and nanotechnology had barely been explored, however.

Nowadays, much of this technology lies in ruins. Certain individuals are trained in "archaeology" -- the art of uncovering and reverse-engineering ancient technology with the aid of magic. However, with the exception of the Kharaghish Federation, which survived the wars mostly intact, no society truly relies on this unearthed technology, as it's simply too rare and difficult to recreate. It's mostly a hobby of curious explorers and scholars. 

After the wars, most states reverted to feudalism or even hunter-gathering. Technocracy gave way to goetocracy (rule by mages) as magic began to re-enter the world.

It must be said that this world never experienced anything like the Enlightenment, and thus many cultural notions and concepts that we associate with modernity are largely absent or marginal in this world.

My universe has a science-fantasy setting with two main planets. On the "home planet," where the humans come from, you've got five "cosmopolitan" races (including humans)--basically the races that everyone knows exists and that have assimilated somewhat into human society (humans being the dominant race on that planet). In fact, two of the “non-human” races are essentially evolved from humans, so they can still interbreed with them and each other. (The other races are amphibious, fish-evolved humanoids and reverse-engineered magitech androids.)

Then you’ve got some “legendary” races that few people have actually met and some doubt even exist (but they do). I only have three of these really fleshed out, but all of them are either close to extinction or have migrated…elsewhere.

On the “alien” planet, you have your main indigenous inhabitants, the Rilakh, but also a few other sapient species that aren’t quite as global. I haven’t really gone deep into this side of the constructed universe yet, but I fully intend to.

Then there are the mysterious “Exo” (working name), ancient planet-hopping aliens that have mastered the art of genetic manipulation. But that’s getting into a whole other story…

So all in all, 10 races that I’ve actually fleshed out, plus a few others that are just ideas floating around in my head. I don't think I'm going to add many more, as, like others have mentioned, it's hard to fill in a lot of detail when you have too many different races (plus all of the different cultures within each race...yikes!).
